InDepthNH.org republishes this news roundup by the Associated Press in partnership with the AP Journalism Fund
By The Associated Press
President Donald Trump opened another chapter in his effort to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook Friday by establishing a “committee of inquiry” to investigate allegations that she made false statements in mortgage applications.
The inquiry will include a hearing at the White House on Nov. 5 and Cook “shall” attend to answer questions from the committee, Trump said in a written memo.
Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on Friday about whether the Pentagon will livestream the execution of the Fort Hood shooter in December, telling reporters he wouldn’t watch it. “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” Vance told reporters. He and Trump have both sought to highlight the shooter’s 2009 attack at Fort Hood where he killed 13 people.
Trump said he has struck a deal to obtain over a million tons of diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow as fuel prices remain high ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it, “a weak decision by strong partners,” and suggested negotiations between the U.S. and Ukraine on how to end the war were “being used as a smoke screen.”
Also, a federal immigration officer shot a Dominican man in the neck as he drove in a car with a 5-year-old boy Thursday afternoon, officials said.
An irate New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani called the shooting an outrage, and spent two hours Thursday night pressing President Donald Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to release the wounded man, and urging them to stop immigration enforcement operations in the city.
Here’s the latest:
Senate Democrats call Trump’s Russian diesel deal a ‘total betrayal’
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, along with Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Banking Committee, said Trump’s announcement is a betrayal of Ukraine, European allies and U.S. national security.
“Enough is enough,” the senators wrote. “The President must end his war with Iran instead of funding Russia’s war machine.”
Trump’s announcement that the U.S. will allow global purchases of Russian diesel was far from what lawmakers expected.
It comes after Congress had overwhelmingly approved legislation, which Trump signed into law last month, to slap steep sanctions on countries that purchase Russian energy that is fueling the war against Ukraine.
Trump’s National Guard deployment raises new fears over voting
National Guard officials in D.C. have directed troops to avoid standing near drop boxes or polling locations after a photo circulated on social media of several guardsmen surrounding a ballot drop box near a Metro station.
The city elections division said it had reached out to the Guard asking they impose limitations on the placement of National Guard service members near drop boxes and other voting locations in the D.C.
More than 2,900 Guard members remain in the city, part of a task force started in August 2025 by Trump to curb crime. D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson said his office had received multiple calls about troops near ballot drop boxes.
“Soldiers standing by our ballot boxes is unnecessary and is fundamentally wrong if we want to encourage voting,” he said.
Fellow Council member Brooke Pinto is planning a public hearing on the deployment next month.
Trump arrives in Syracuse to rally with Blakeman
The president is in New York for an event supporting Bruce Blakeman, a Republican ally who is trying to unseat Democratic incumbent Gov. Kathy Hochul.
Trump arrived on Air Force One and is headed to a rally where Blakeman has been speaking to supporters.
Blakeman has embraced Trump even as Republicans look to capture centrists in a state where Democrats outnumber Republicans by more than 2-to-1.
The Nassau County executive has played up fears about immigrant criminals and depicted the state as dangerous and unaffordable.
DCCC puts out fundraising call for next tier potential House pickups
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee says an infusion of $17 million by Oct. 22 could help the party win at least six additional Republican-held seats, according to a memo from the group’s finance director obtained by The Associated Press.
The committee is eyeing another roughly dozen districts in addition to the 17 where it has focused its campaign money.
A U.S. Supreme Court decision in June held that political parties and their affiliated groups could contribute directly to candidate’s campaigns, reversing the previous ban. Democratic House campaign leaders are arguing that the extra money could lift the handful of Democratic House candidates, in part because the money going directly to candidates would go further in light of lower rates charged to campaigns. Super PACs are charged higher rates.
The districts include one in south Florida where three-term Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar has criticized President Donald Trump’s immigration enforcement as “going too far.”
Trump thanks Putin for help on diesel
Trump said his arrangement with his Russian counterpart for diesel exports — coming weeks before the midterm elections — is “a big deal.”
“That is massive amounts of oil coming into our country,” he said as he left the White House heading to Syracuse, New York, for rally.
“I want to thank President Putin. To be honest with you, we have massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and it’s diesel, which is what we want. So, thank you.”
Trump did not answer shouted questions about criticism from Zelenskyy, who called it a “weak decision” and said the deal would give Putin more money “to inflict suffering on us” in the ongoing war.
Senators urge Pentagon to reverse ‘gruesome’ decision to livestream execution
Sen. Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Intelligence Committee, condemned Hegseth’s plan, saying there’s a reason why “almost no countries in the world engage in this barbaric practice.”
“Public executions are the hallmark of authoritarian regimes like Iran and North Korea, not the United States of America,” Warner said.
“Beyond the profound moral concerns, a public execution could hand terrorist organizations a propaganda victory,” he said, and put U.S. service members and others overseas at risk.
Republican Sen. John Curtis of Utah pointed to Rome’s bloody spectacles and said a “civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment.”
“Secretary Hegseth’s plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite,” Curtis said. “I urge him to reconsider.”
GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska said how the U.S. carries out justice matters.
“I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America,” she said. “I urge the Pentagon to reverse this gruesome decision.”
Trump approves of Hasan’s execution by firing squad
Trump says he approves of Hasan’s execution by firing squad.
The Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in 2009 at Fort Hood in Texas is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3.
The Pentagon had announced on Thursday that it plans to livestream the execution. It would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961.
“He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad,” Trump told reporters before flying to Syracuse, New York, for a political event. “I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him.”
Trump did not appear to answer when asked whether it was appropriate to livestream the event or whether he was going to watch the execution.
Zelenskyy says negotiators are being ‘used as a smoke screen’ amid US-Russia diesel deal
Zelenskyy called the deal Trump struck to obtain diesel from Russia, “a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners,” according to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington.
Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials to discuss a proposal to try to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” Zelenskyy said.
? Read more
Trump says he’ll rally with Mike Tyson
The president appeared with the former heavyweight champion as he left the White House to fly to his rally on Friday night in Syracuse, New York.
“This is Iron Mike Tyson,” Trump told reporters gathered on the White House lawn for his departure, before joking, “I won’t be fighting him today.”
Trump noted that he and Tyson have “been friends for a long time” and the crowd will “be happy to see Mike.”
Tyson was convicted of rape in 1992, and served three years in prison.
Steve Hilton, running for California governor, helps pay for people’s gas at gas station
The event in Los Angeles was meant to bring attention to the candidate’s promise to lower California’s highest-in-the-nation gas prices to $3 a gallon. The average rate in the state stood at $6.33 per gallon Friday, according to AAA.
“This is a preview of what you get when I’m governor,” he told a driver in a video posted to his X page.
Hilton, a former Fox News host who’s running against Democrat Xavier Becerra, has blamed Democratic leadership for the state’s notoriously high cost of living.
He’s making a final push to appeal to voters with mail ballots being sent out ahead of the Nov. 3 deadline to vote.
JUST IN: Zelenskyy calls US-Russia diesel deal ‘a weak decision’ and says negotiators are being ‘used as a smoke screen’Pro-Israel super PAC begins to spend against Abdul El-Sayed
The United Democracy Project, a super PAC affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, has begun spending against Michigan’s Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. The spending was revealed in a filing late Friday, and is only $94,000 to start.
The group spent close to $30 million against El-Sayed — a vocal critic of Israel — in his Democratic primary against Rep. Haley Stevens. Until Friday, the group had stayed out of the general election race. During a Senate debate Thursday, El-Sayed’s opponent, Mike Rogers, signaled he would accept AIPAC’s support when asked directly about it.
A spokesperson for AIPAC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Trump chooses Katie Zacharia to be new press secretary
The president said conservative commentator Katie Zacharia, a communications adviser for Trump’s media company, will replace Karoline Leavitt as the chief spokesperson for the White House.
Trump announced the hire in a social media post on Friday, describing Zacharia as “a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning.”
Zacharia briefly worked as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security earlier this year and has been a commentator for Fox News and Newsmax. Trump said she was previously involved in his campaigns and helped in key swing states.
A request for comment left with Zacharia was not immediately answered. Her LinkedIn says she has a law degree from Pepperdine University.
Trump promises to ‘visit’ both Alabama and Georgia football teams later
The president has now formally confirmed that Hurricane Isaias means he won’t be attending Saturday night’s Alabama-Georgia football game.
He wrote on his social media site on Friday that “based on the fact that a huge Hurricane/Storm is coming, it is important to have our wonderful First Responders, Law Enforcement, and others, focused on that Storm, and in no way be thinking about the safety, or presence, of the President of the United States, ME!”
“Therefore, I will miss that potentially unbelievable Game, Alabama vs. Georgia,” Trump continued. “But, hopefully, the Game will go on despite the weather!”
He also promised, without providing details, “I will be visiting both of those Teams at a later date.”
Trump scraps plan to attend Alabama football game as hurricane nears Gulf Coast
The president will no longer be attending Saturday’s football game between the University of Alabama and the University of Georgia, according to a White House official speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss internal planning.
Trump had been planning to travel to Tuscaloosa for the rivalry clash after a rally planned in Tennessee on Saturday. Asked about the impact of the storm on Wednesday said “I gotta go to the game” but said his plans might change based on the weather.
Trump had said he did not want to divert resources from the emergency response.

sources.news_title: Trump cooks up new ploy against Fed governor he’s been trying to fire for months
sources.text:
President Donald Trump has opened a new front in his yearlong effort to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, ordering a formal inquiry into allegations that she made false statements on mortgage documents — a move that could intensify the battle over the central bank’s independence just weeks before the midterm elections.
In a presidential memorandum dated October 7, Trump established a committee of inquiry to investigate the allegations and determine whether there is sufficient cause to remove Cook from the Federal Reserve’s Board of Governors. The committee is scheduled to hold a closed-door hearing at the White House on November 5, when Cook will be required to appear and answer questions.
Cook has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime. Her lawyers say a fair examination of the evidence will demonstrate that there is no legal basis for removing her.
“Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her,” her attorneys, Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen, said in a statement.
The inquiry marks another escalation in Trump’s extraordinary campaign against a sitting Fed governor. He first sought to fire Cook in August 2025, alleging that she improperly identified two properties as primary residences on mortgage applications. Mortgages for primary residences can carry more favorable terms than loans for second homes or investment properties.
Cook’s lawyers have previously characterized the issue as an inadvertent error and pointed to other documents in which one of the properties was identified as a vacation home.
The committee will be led by senior Trump administration officials, including White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett. It will examine the allegations and recommend whether they provide grounds for Cook’s removal. The hearing will not be open to the public, although the administration says it will be transcribed.
The timing and structure of the inquiry are likely to draw scrutiny. The president’s committee will investigate allegations against an official whose removal Trump has already sought, and it will report its findings directly to him.
That raises a broader question: whether the administration is applying a neutral legal standard or using an investigation to advance a political objective.
The Federal Reserve is designed to operate with a degree of independence from the White House. That independence allows policymakers to make decisions about interest rates and inflation even when those decisions conflict with a president’s political preferences.
Trump has repeatedly pressed the central bank to lower interest rates. His effort to remove Cook has therefore become part of a larger confrontation over the president’s authority and the limits designed to protect the Fed from political interference.
The Supreme Court addressed the dispute earlier this year, ruling that the president must establish adequate cause and follow a proper process to remove a Fed governor. The court left Cook in office and returned the case to a lower court.
The new inquiry gives Trump’s administration another opportunity to build its case. But an investigation is not a finding of wrongdoing, and the allegations against Cook remain disputed.
The committee is scheduled to hold its hearing on November 5. Cook may submit a written statement before the hearing and provide additional material afterward, with the committee then expected to deliver its findings and recommendation to Trump.
Whether that process establishes a legitimate basis for removal — or deepens concerns that the White House is trying to bring the Federal Reserve under presidential control — will be central to the next stage of the fight.

sources.text:
President Donald Trump simply can’t stop trying to vindictively investigate and prosecute people.
His latest target is a repeat victim: Lisa Cook, who still has her job on the Federal Reserve Board—much to Trump’s chagrin.
Part of what highlights just how weird and dystopian this is—and how much this is still just Trump going after Cook rather than a normal investigation—is that Trump announced the investigation, to be conducted by an official committee established by the White House, with a formal White House memo.
This is not, of course, how actual investigations work. They aren’t demanded by the president posting a little note to the attorney general; they’re conducted with deliberation and independence from the president.
But since there’s no daylight between Trump and the Justice Department these days, here we are.
And just as Trump picked a familiar target, he used a familiar tactic. Yes, it’s mortgage fraud.
It isn’t just that this is a retread of his earlier accusations against Cook, but it’s also the same thing he tried with New York Attorney General Letitia James, who never got to address that accusation fully because the laughable indictment got thrown out along with the laughable Lindsey Halligan.
There’s also the whole thing where the mortgage documents themselves undercut the allegations against Cook—also similar to how the hype over James’ alleged mortgage fraud was nonsense.
Trump continues to insist that Cook committed fraud by trying to pass off her second home as her main residence. Sure, except that the documents themselves show that Cook said it would be used as a vacation home—and also that she never tried to obtain the tax exemption she would have been entitled to for a primary residence.
So she didn’t lie on the mortgage application, and she didn’t lie to the Internal Revenue Service, but somehow she’s still under investigation. That doesn’t look vindictive at all.
Related | Trump targets another powerful Black woman—and she’s not having it
What makes Trump’s continued quest to bring down Cook even more grotesque than his efforts to punish former FBI Director James Comey or to bring down James or even his brand new attacks on former aide Cassidy Hutchinson, is that the only thing that Cook did wrong, in Trump’s eyes, is be on the Fed board when he doesn’t want her to be.
Well, that and being a Black woman, because Trump is a bone-deep racist who thinks “meritocracy” means hiring people like Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Even though Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts wanted to salvage some part of his tattered reputation by voting, ridiculously, in favor of letting Trump arbitrarily fire everyone while also voting against letting Trump arbitrarily fire Cook, Roberts is still the one to thank for this behavior.
If he hadn’t given Trump sweet, sweet immunity from criminal prosecutions for any “official acts”—which he made so comically broad—Trump would have to worry about consequences for going after Cook for no reason. But he doesn’t have to worry about that at all.
And going after her “arbitrarily” is the key here. All that the Supreme Court told Trump was that he needed a reason to fire Fed board members, not that he couldn’t do so. That’s in contrast to everyone else, who Trump can now fire just based on vibes.
So Trump was required to offer Cook some sort of due process before firing her, but the only process she’s being afforded here is that Trump “may submit a written position statement to the Committee regarding the allegations.”
To be fair, that is an improvement over the due process that the administration previously argued Cook was owed—which was none, save for that she was supposed to read Trump’s Truth Social post where he fired her.
Maybe Trump should send Roberts a fruit basket or something as a thank you. Really, it’s the least he could do.

sources.news_title: Trump launches fresh bid to remove Fed Governor Lisa Cook — White House hearing scheduled for November 5
sources.text:
President Donald Trump has escalated his efforts to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook by establishing a “committee of inquiry” to investigate allegations that she made false statements on mortgage applications.
In a written memorandum issued on Friday (October 9), Trump announced that the inquiry would include a hearing at the White House on November 5, which Cook “shall” attend to answer questions from the committee. The hearing will not be open to the public, but a transcript will be published, according to the memorandum.
The move marks another significant development in Trump’s campaign against Cook and is likely to intensify concerns over the independence of the US central bank.
Trump justified the inquiry by arguing that his responsibility as president includes ensuring that government officials comply with the law.
“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump wrote in the memorandum.
The committee will examine whether the allegations against Cook establish sufficient “cause” for her removal, as required under the law governing the Federal Reserve.
Cook has denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime. Her attorneys, Abbe Lowell and Norman Eisen, said they were evaluating whether she should appear at the November 5 hearing and respond to the allegations.
“We have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise,” the attorneys said in a statement.
They added that Cook welcomed the opportunity to present evidence in her defence.
“Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her,” they said.
The allegations stem from mortgage applications submitted in 2021, in which Cook allegedly identified two different properties as her primary residence. Mortgages on primary residences can carry lower interest rates and other favourable terms.
Cook’s lawyers have previously described the issue as an inadvertent error, noting that one of the properties was identified as a vacation home in other documents.
“An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing,” Lowell and Eisen said in August.
The committee of inquiry will include three members: Kevin Hassett, Trump’s top economic adviser; Keith Sonderling, acting director of the Office of Government Ethics; and Andrea Lucas, chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.
Hassett has frequently echoed Trump’s criticism of the Federal Reserve. Sonderling has also been appointed by Trump to lead the Labor Department, while Lucas was appointed to her position in November 2025.
The composition of the panel could draw further scrutiny because its members hold positions within the administration and include an adviser who has publicly aligned with the president’s criticism of the central bank.
Trump’s campaign against Cook has intensified broader concerns about political interference in monetary policy. The President has repeatedly urged the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates, while the central bank raised its key rate on September 16, according to the account of the decision.
The rate increase was unanimous, despite Trump and some of his economic advisers blaming the Fed’s rate-setting committee for the decision.
Cook is one of the 12 voting members of the Federal Open Market Committee, which determines US monetary policy. She was appointed by former President Joe Biden and is the first Black woman to serve on the Federal Reserve’s seven-member Board of Governors.
The latest development follows a Supreme Court ruling in June that allowed Cook to remain in office after Trump attempted to dismiss her in 2025.
The ruling included a footnote stating that nothing prevented the President from “trying again,” provided Cook received proper notice and an opportunity to respond to the allegations.
However, the court also indicated that removal for cause would require an alleged offence that was serious and related to an official’s duties.

sources.news_title: Trump Creates Committee to Investigate Fed Governor Lisa Cook’s Mortgage Statements
Trump announces committee investigation of Fed Governor Lisa Cook
sources.text:
President Donald Trump on Friday announced the creation of a three-person committee to investigate allegations of mortgage fraud against Lisa Cook, a member of the Federal Reserve’s Board of Governors. The news came in a notice that was published on the White House website just over two months after Trump notified Cook that he was considering her removal, and less than four months after a divided Supreme Court blocked Trump’s initial efforts to fire Cook.
“As President,” Trump wrote, “it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law.”
Cook has strongly contested the mortgage fraud allegations, and other financial records appear to undermine the Trump administration’s claims.
The dispute began more than a year ago, when Trump posted screenshots on social media of a letter to Cook in which he fired her. Trump alleged that Cook, who began serving on the Fed in 2022 and was nominated to a full 14-year term by then-President Joe Biden in 2023, had committed mortgage fraud in 2021 by listing two different homes – a condo in Georgia and a house in Michigan – as her primary residence on mortgage applications, making her eligible for more favorable terms.
The lower courts allowed Cook to remain in office while she challenged Trump’s decision. U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb concluded that Cook was “substantially likely” to show that Trump had violated federal law when he fired her because the law allowing the president to fire a Federal Reserve governor “for cause” does not extend to removing a board member for her conduct before she took office. The firing also violated Cook’s constitutional right to fair treatment, Cobb said, because she did not have notice and an opportunity to contest her firing before it occurred.
A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit left Cobb’s order in place while Cook’s challenge continued. The majority agreed that Cook was likely to succeed on her claim that she did not receive all of the procedural protections to which she was entitled under the due process clause of the Constitution before she was fired.
The Trump administration went to the Supreme Court, asking it to pause Cobb’s order. But the justices declined to do so, instead setting the case for argument in January 2026.
By a vote of 5-4, the court on June 29 once again allowed Cook to remain in office while her challenge continued. Writing for the majority, Chief Justice John Roberts explained that (among other things), “the President failed to afford Cook the procedural protections to which she was entitled by statute. Without such protections, she could not properly dispute the charges the President laid against her.”
In the wake of the court’s decision, in a letter dated Aug. 5, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Dan Scavino notified Cook that Trump was “considering” whether to remove her from the Board of Governors. Scavino gave Cook 21 days to respond to the White House’s mortgage fraud allegations.
In her response on Aug. 27, Cook’s attorney, Abbe Lowell, told Trump that the allegations against her were “unfounded and untrue.” Therefore, he said, any effort to fire Cook based on those allegations would be “corrosive of the independence that Congress sought to preserve” for the Federal Reserve Bank.
The notice that Trump released on Friday designated three senior officials in the Trump administration to serve on the newly formed committee: Kevin Hassett, the Assistant to the President for Economic Policy; Andrea Lucas, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, who serves as the acting director of the Office of Government Ethics (as well as the Secretary of Labor).
Trump’s notice instructed the committee to hold a hearing, which will not be open to the public, at the White House on Nov. 5. At that hearing, Trump said, the members of the committee may question Cook, while she will also have the opportunity to present arguments and evidence. If Cook opts to submit a post-hearing statement, he added, it is due by Nov. 10, and the committee should “submit written findings of fact and conclusions of law to me” and make a recommendation regarding whether Cook should be removed “[a]s soon as practicable after” that.

Trump has squabbled with Cook and former Fed Chair Jerome Powell, whom he appointed and who still serves on the board, over interest rates that the president believes should be lower to stimulate the economy.
He has used legal investigations to pressure Cook and Powell, including a probe into Powell’s oversight of a Fed headquarters renovation.

sources.news_title: Trump tries—yet again—to fire Fed Governor Lisa Cook
sources.text:
On Friday, President Donald Trump announced the creation of a new committee to investigate Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook over allegations of mortgage fraud, even after those claims were shown to be incorrect, and after the US Supreme Court in June rejected his previous attempts to fire her.
In a written memo, Trump announced that this new committee will hold a hearing at the White House two days after the midterm elections in November and demanded that Cook show up to testify. Trump’s ongoing effort to oust Cook represents the first time the president has tried to fire a member of the Fed’s board in more than a century, since the central bank was established as an independent entity that sets monetary policy free of political influence.
“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump wrote in the memo. “To assist me in carrying out that responsibility, the Committee shall investigate the allegations against Governor Cook and report to me whether there is ’cause’ for Governor Cook’s removal.”
This is the latest development in a saga that began more than a year ago, when Trump loyalist Bill Pulte—the head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA)—leveled thin accusations of mortgage fraud against Cook and other prominent Democrats who have clashed with Trump.
Since the beginning of his second term, Trump has fumed that the Fed won’t lower interest rates, a move that would ease the costs of borrowing money for homes and businesses—and make some voters happy ahead of the midterms.
Then, in August 2025, Pulte—a vigorous defender of the president that some have called a “mini-Trump”—claimed in a social media post that Cook had designated two homes as her primary residence simultaneously in order to get a better mortgage rate. Pulte posted screenshots of Cook’s mortgage applications on social media when making these claims, raising questions of whether he was using his position atop the FHFA—which oversees mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac—to access private housing loan information on Trump’s political foes.
Pulte referred Cook for criminal prosecution by the Justice Department and Trump piled on, saying the allegation was enough to fire her. But no criminal case ever materialized. Additional loan documents showed that the alleged mortgage fraud was instead probably a clerical error. What’s more, Pulte’s efforts to weaponize mortgage information against Trump’s political foes led to formal scrutiny: The Government Accountability office said it is investigating whether Pulte misused his position to access mortgage data, and the FHFA’s inspector general is also reportedly looking into his conduct.
Reporters also found that Trump himself and others in his cabinet appear to have made similar errors to Cook in their own mortgage applications. Cook sued over the attempt to fire her, and two separate courts blocked her removal. Trump appealed to the Supreme Court, which also said the way he’d tried to fire her was not allowed.
But that Supreme Court ruling did not bar Trump from trying to fire Cook again. Trump has every reason to attempt a redo: American dissatisfaction with the US economy and historic inflation is at an all-time high ahead of November’s elections, and Trump’s appointee to run the Fed, Kevin Warsh, recently raised rates instead of lowering them. Trump’s announcement on Friday appears to be his latest effort to exert some control over the central bank by ousting Cook, which would enable him to appoint a loyalist in her place.

sources.news_title: Trump Orders White House Investigation Into Fed Governor Lisa Cook, Schedules November Hearing on Mortgage Allegations
sources.text:
President Donald Trump has appointed a three-member committee to investigate allegations that Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook made false statements on mortgage documents, reopening his effort to remove her after the Supreme Court ruled that she must receive adequate notice and an opportunity to defend herself.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump announced Friday the formation of a special White House committee to investigate Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook over allegations of false statements on mortgage documents, establishing a formal hearing process that could lead to another attempt to remove her from the central bank’s governing board.
The three-member committee will examine the accusations and conduct a closed-door hearing Nov. 5, two days after the midterm elections. Cook will be required to answer questions about the mortgage transactions, submit any evidence supporting her defense and respond to the committee’s findings before it makes a recommendation to the president.
The announcement, contained in an Oct. 7 presidential memorandum published by the White House on Friday, represents Trump’s latest effort to remove Cook following a June Supreme Court ruling that prevented him from dismissing her without providing adequate procedural protections.
Cook has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime. Her attorneys questioned whether the administration can provide an impartial hearing after Trump repeatedly expressed his intention to fire her, while Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, accused the president of pursuing a predetermined outcome to increase White House influence over monetary policy.
The dispute raises an important legal question concerning the president’s authority over the Federal Reserve, whose governors serve lengthy terms and may be removed only for cause under federal law. No president has successfully removed a sitting governor from the central bank’s board during the Federal Reserve’s 113-year history.
Trump’s new inquiry seeks to establish whether Cook’s alleged conduct satisfies that statutory standard, which was central to the Supreme Court’s decision earlier this year. The president maintains that he has a constitutional responsibility to ensure that federal officials comply with the law and act honestly in positions of public trust.
“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump wrote in the memorandum.
The president directed the committee to investigate Cook’s mortgage-related statements and determine whether the evidence establishes sufficient grounds for her removal from the Federal Reserve Board of Governors. The committee may consult with the Justice Department and other executive agencies while reviewing relevant documents, testimony and legal arguments.
Its members are Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council and one of Trump’s principal economic advisers; Andrea Lucas, chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, acting director of the Office of Government Ethics.
All three serve in senior positions within the Trump administration. Their selection has generated criticism from Cook’s supporters, who argue that officials appointed by the president may have difficulty conducting an independent assessment when he has already declared that the governor should be removed.
The administration has not described the proceeding as a criminal trial. Rather, it is an executive inquiry intended to determine whether the legal grounds exist for removing a Federal Reserve official before the expiration of her term.
Under the memorandum, the hearing will take place at the White House and last no longer than four hours. It will be closed to the public but transcribed, creating a formal record of the evidence considered and the questions asked.
Cook may submit a written statement addressing the allegations at least three days before the hearing. She may also present documentary evidence, legal arguments and written witness statements, while the committee is authorized to question her or her attorneys about the information provided.
The administration must supply Cook with the evidence it intends to consider before the hearing. Afterward, she will have until Nov. 10 to submit an additional written response before the committee completes its findings and sends a recommendation to Trump.
The committee will then prepare written findings of fact and conclusions of law addressing whether Cook’s conduct meets the statutory definition of cause for removal. The memorandum does not set a specific deadline for the final recommendation but directs the panel to submit its conclusions as soon as practicable after receiving Cook’s post-hearing statement.
Trump’s instructions also permit the committee to adjust its procedures when necessary, provided Cook receives adequate notice of any changes. Whether those arrangements satisfy the requirements identified by the Supreme Court could become an issue in further litigation.
The Associated Press reported Friday that Cook’s attorneys are evaluating the administration’s proposed procedures and remain concerned that the president has already reached a conclusion about the allegations.
Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen, who represent Cook, expressed skepticism about the legitimacy of the process and whether it would provide a meaningful opportunity to contest the accusations.
They said they have “grave doubts that this ‘hearing’ is a legitimate one that would conform to the law,” citing Trump’s previous statements about removing Cook regardless of the outcome of additional proceedings.
“We have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise,” Lowell and Eisen said.
The attorneys nevertheless indicated that Cook intends to defend herself and challenge the administration’s allegations through the process if it provides a legitimate opportunity to present evidence.
They added that Cook “welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her.”
The dispute stems from mortgage applications Cook completed several years before joining the Federal Reserve. Federal Housing Finance Agency officials alleged in 2025 that she made conflicting representations about properties in Michigan and Georgia, raising questions about whether she improperly identified more than one residence as her primary home.
Mortgage lenders frequently distinguish between primary residences, second homes and investment properties because those classifications can affect interest rates, down payment requirements and other loan conditions. Knowingly providing materially false information to obtain a mortgage can carry legal consequences, depending on the circumstances and applicable law.
However, inconsistent statements in mortgage documents do not automatically establish criminal fraud. Investigators must consider whether a representation was knowingly false, whether it was material to the transaction and whether the available evidence satisfies the relevant legal requirements.
Cook has disputed the allegations and maintained that the administration has no lawful basis to remove her. Her attorneys have characterized the mortgage-document discrepancy as an inadvertent oversight rather than an intentional effort to deceive lenders.
The transactions occurred in 2021, before Cook was appointed to the Federal Reserve by President Joe Biden in 2022. She was subsequently reappointed in 2023 to a term extending through January 2038.
The timing of the alleged conduct is significant because the administration is attempting to determine whether actions taken before Cook joined the central bank can qualify as cause for removing her from a position protected by federal statute.
The Federal Reserve Act provides that members of the Board of Governors are appointed for staggered 14-year terms, subject to removal by the president for cause. The statute is intended to limit the ability of a president to replace policymakers simply because they disagree with the administration’s preferred interest-rate decisions.
Unlike Cabinet secretaries and many other executive branch officials, Federal Reserve governors do not ordinarily serve at the president’s pleasure. Their fixed terms and statutory removal protections are components of the central bank’s institutional independence.
Those protections have become central to Trump’s dispute with Cook. The president previously attempted to dismiss her in August 2025 after the allegations were raised publicly, arguing that the mortgage documents demonstrated conduct incompatible with continued service on the board.
Cook challenged the dismissal in federal court, maintaining that the president lacked a valid statutory basis for her removal and had not provided adequate notice or an opportunity to respond before attempting to terminate her appointment.
The case eventually reached the Supreme Court, which ruled in June 2026 that Cook could remain in her position because the administration had failed to provide the procedural protections necessary before removing a Federal Reserve governor.
The justices’ decision did not establish that a sitting governor could never be dismissed, nor did it resolve whether the mortgage allegations would ultimately qualify as cause under federal law.
Instead, the ruling required the administration to follow an appropriate process and provide Cook an opportunity to answer the accusations before a removal decision could take effect.
The Court also left open the possibility that Trump could renew his effort if he complied with those requirements. The administration subsequently sent Cook formal notice that the president was considering her removal and allowed her time to respond.
Cook submitted a written defense disputing the allegations and arguing that they did not provide a lawful basis for dismissal. The new committee and November hearing represent the next stage of that process.
According to reporting by CBS News on the renewed investigation, the committee will focus on whether the alleged mortgage statements meet the legal definition of cause required to remove a governor, rather than independently determining criminal liability.
Legal specialists have questioned whether alleged misconduct predating a Federal Reserve appointment can justify removal, particularly when the official has not been charged with or convicted of a crime.
Others have noted that the governing statute does not comprehensively define cause, leaving courts to determine how the standard applies to particular allegations.
The distinction between an executive removal proceeding and a criminal prosecution is important. The administration may argue that conduct raises questions about an official’s fitness for public office without obtaining a criminal conviction, but any removal decision would still need to satisfy the applicable legal requirements.
Cook’s attorneys are expected to argue that the accusations do not meet that threshold and that the president’s repeated statements demonstrate a predetermined effort to remove her.
Warren, who serves as the senior Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, condemned the latest action as an attempt to circumvent the Supreme Court’s ruling and weaken the central bank’s independence.
She accused Trump of convening “an illegitimate show trial” designed to obtain the result the administration was previously unable to secure through litigation.
The Massachusetts senator has repeatedly criticized efforts to influence Federal Reserve personnel and interest-rate decisions, arguing that the central bank must be able to make monetary policy without political retaliation against its officials.
Her response reflects a broader concern among some lawmakers and economists that allowing presidents to remove governors over contested allegations could weaken the statutory protections intended to insulate monetary policy from immediate political demands.
The White House maintains that its actions concern the legal standards governing federal officials and allegations of dishonesty, not a disagreement over interest rates.
Nevertheless, the investigation is taking place amid a prolonged dispute between Trump and the Federal Reserve over the direction of monetary policy.
The president has repeatedly argued that the central bank should reduce borrowing costs, saying elevated interest rates place unnecessary pressure on households, businesses and the federal government’s financing expenses.
Federal Reserve officials have maintained that their decisions must account for inflation, employment conditions and economic stability rather than short-term political preferences.
The tension has continued under Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, whom Trump appointed earlier this year. The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate in September, a decision that frustrated administration officials who had favored lower borrowing costs.
Cook is one of the voting members of the Federal Open Market Committee, the body responsible for setting the central bank’s principal short-term interest-rate target. The committee includes members of the Board of Governors and representatives of regional Federal Reserve banks.
Although a single governor cannot determine monetary policy independently, the composition of the board matters because governors participate in interest-rate decisions, bank supervision and other central bank responsibilities.
Removing Cook would create a vacancy that Trump could seek to fill through the nomination process, subject to Senate confirmation. A replacement could influence future monetary policy discussions and regulatory decisions, although the outcome would depend on the views of the nominee and other committee members.
Those consequences have added significance to the legal dispute because the White House is pursuing Cook’s removal at a time when it has publicly criticized Federal Reserve decisions.
The administration’s broader disagreements with the central bank have also involved former Chair Jerome Powell, who faced a criminal investigation related to cost overruns in a Federal Reserve renovation project.
The investigation prompted questions about whether the Justice Department was being used to pressure central bank officials, although administration representatives defended the inquiry as a legitimate examination of government expenditures.
A government watchdog subsequently cleared Powell of criminal wrongdoing in connection with the project, and Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Justice Department would not reopen the investigation.
Those developments form part of the wider debate about presidential oversight of the Federal Reserve and the limits of executive authority over independent institutions.
The Federal Reserve occupies a distinctive position within the federal government. It was established by Congress in 1913 and carries out monetary policy responsibilities that can have significant consequences for inflation, employment, financial markets and consumer borrowing costs.
Its governors are appointed by the president and confirmed by the Senate, but their lengthy terms are designed to extend beyond individual presidential administrations.
The structure does not place the central bank entirely outside democratic oversight. Congress establishes its legal authority, receives testimony from Federal Reserve leaders and can amend the statutes governing its operations.
The president also influences the institution through appointments when board vacancies arise.
However, restrictions on removing sitting governors are intended to reduce the possibility that monetary policy decisions will be driven by direct threats to officials’ employment.
That principle is now being tested by a dispute involving allegations of conduct unrelated to Cook’s work at the central bank.
The administration argues that the president must be able to dismiss officials who cannot be trusted to comply with the law. Cook’s legal team maintains that the accusations are unsubstantiated and that the attempted dismissal is inconsistent with the protections Congress established for Federal Reserve governors.
The Supreme Court’s June decision required a meaningful opportunity for Cook to respond, but questions remain about what procedural safeguards are necessary and whether the committee established by Trump satisfies them.
The planned hearing is scheduled to take place privately rather than in a courtroom or before Congress. Cook may be accompanied by legal counsel, but the members conducting the examination are senior administration officials appointed by the president seeking her removal.
The memorandum does not provide for an independent judge to preside over the hearing, and it permits the committee to seek assistance from Justice Department personnel.
The committee will ultimately recommend whether the president has cause to remove Cook, leaving Trump to decide how to proceed after reviewing the findings.
Any renewed removal decision could prompt additional litigation, potentially returning the dispute to federal courts and eventually the Supreme Court.
Such proceedings would likely focus on the evidence supporting the allegations, the legal meaning of cause and whether Cook received the process required by federal law and the Court’s earlier ruling.
The November timetable also places the hearing shortly after the midterm elections, although the administration has not identified the election schedule as a reason for selecting the date.
Cook’s lawyers will have the opportunity to review the committee’s evidence and determine how to present her defense before the hearing. Their public statements suggest that they intend to challenge both the factual allegations and the legitimacy of the procedures.
The White House has not announced any decision to remove Cook following the establishment of the inquiry. The committee must first complete its review and submit a recommendation.
For now, Cook remains a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors and continues to hold the position to which she was appointed.
The next major development is expected Nov. 5, when the committee convenes at the White House to examine the mortgage allegations. Cook will then have until Nov. 10 to provide a final written response before the panel prepares its conclusions.
The outcome could determine whether Trump makes another attempt to dismiss a sitting Federal Reserve governor and whether the courts must further clarify the limits of presidential authority over the central bank.
The dispute is unprecedented in the Federal Reserve’s history, not because federal officials are immune from investigation, but because no president has previously succeeded in removing a sitting governor under the statutory cause standard.
Trump’s committee has been directed to determine whether the evidence against Cook meets that standard. Cook denies wrongdoing and is preparing to challenge the allegations, while lawmakers and legal specialists continue debating whether the administration can conduct a sufficiently independent proceeding.
Until the committee reaches its findings and any subsequent legal challenges are resolved, the effort to remove Cook remains an unresolved confrontation over executive authority, statutory protections and the independence of the institution responsible for U.S. monetary policy.

President Trump has launched a probe into Federal Reserve Gov. Lisa Cook over mortgage fraud allegations, the White House announced Friday. The move appears aimed at removing Cook from the post following an unfavorable Supreme Court ruling on the matter earlier this year.
“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump wrote in Friday’s presidential memoranda.
The directive establishes a committee comprised of the president’s assistant for economic policy, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission chair, and the director of the Office of Government Ethics that will investigate allegations that Cook, a Biden appointee, “made false statements in connection with one or more mortgage instruments.” The group will subsequently report to the president “whether there is ’cause’ for Governor Cook’s removal within the meaning” of federal law “as construed” in the Supreme Court’s Trump v. Cook (2026) decision.
Trump first sought to fire Cook over these allegations in August 2025, but was blocked by D.C. District Judge Jib Cobb, a Biden appointee. The administration ultimately filed an emergency application asking the Supreme Court to temporarily permit Cook’s removal while litigation over her firing continued. The high court rejected the government’s request in Trump v. Cook.
Writing for the 5-4 majority, Chief Justice John Roberts ruled there must be “cause” to fire Cook, and she must be afforded an “opportunity to respond to the charges made against her … [before] a final decision [can] be made.” The majority declined to rule on “the ultimate question” of whether Trump can remove Cook “for cause,” arguing such a decision “will depend in part on the underlying facts” that must first “be found or analyzed under the relevant legal standards.”
The court’s decision prompted stinging dissents from Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito (joined by Neil Gorsuch), and Amy Coney Barrett. Thomas noted “[a]pparent mortgage fraud was a ’cause’ to remove Cook” and underscored a point he raised during oral arguments — that “the statute authorizing the President to remove Cook for ’cause’ says nothing about notice or a hearing, so it does not require notice and a hearing.” The senior justice also argued the federal courts lack the authority to “enter the relief” the Cook majority upheld with its decision and further admonished the majority for infringing on the president’s executive removal powers.
Alito (and Gorsuch) argued that Trump showed a likelihood of success on the preliminary questions of whether “for cause” removal applies to pre-office conduct and whether he violated Cook’s due process rights. Meanwhile, Barrett blasted the majority for deciding significant legal matters that had not been fully briefed or contested, as well as the “disconnect between its holding and its disposition line.”
[READ: John Roberts: Presidents Have Executive Power. Also John Roberts: No, They Don’t]
Following the constraints established in Cook, Trump has directed the newly formed committee to “conduct an in-person hearing to consider the evidence and allegations against Governor Cook” on Nov. 5. The hearing will last “no longer than 4 hours,” according to the memoranda.
The directive also grants Cook the ability to file a written statement with the committee contesting the allegations, so long as it is submitted at least three days in advance. While the Biden appointee will be given the opportunity to “present argument, written evidence, and written witness statements regarding the evidence and allegations,” the committee will be afforded the chance to “question Governor Cook about any representations she or her counsel make during the hearing, or it may authorize its representatives, including Department of Justice personnel, to conduct that questioning.”
Cook and her team will be presented the evidence against her prior to the hearing. The committee may also request Cook turn over “documents or other evidentiary submissions … as appropriate,” which Cook is instructed to comply with. The hearing will not be broadcast to the public “but shall be transcribed,” according to the directive.

By CHRISTOPHER RUGABER, AP Economics Writer
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump opened another chapter in his effort to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook Friday by establishing a “committee of inquiry” to investigate allegations that she made false statements in mortgage applications.
The inquiry will include a hearing at the White House Nov. 5, Trump said in a written memo, that Cook “shall” attend to answer questions from the committee. The hearing wouldn’t be public but a transcript would be published, the memo said.
Trump’s extraordinary demand that Cook testify before the committee will likely renew concerns about threats to the Federal Reserve’s independence. The president has repeatedly called for the central bank to cut its key interest rate, but just last month, the Fed raised it instead, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom Trump appointed earlier this year.
Trump’s attempts to fire Cook from the Fed’s seven-member board of governors represent the first time in the central bank’s 113-year history that a president has sought to remove a Fed governor. Cook was appointed by former President Joe Biden and is the first Black woman on the Fed’s board. Trump’s attacks on her followed other efforts to oust or indict Black officials, such as New York Attorney General Letitia James and Gen. Charles Q. Brown, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump wrote in the memorandum.
Cook’s attorneys, Abbe Lowell and Norman Eisen, said they were considering having Cook appear at the Nov. 5 hearing and respond to the charges.
“We have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise,” Lowell and Eisen said in a statement. “Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her.”

Trump initially tried to fire Cook in August 2025 after alleging she had committed mortgage fraud by declaring two different properties to be her “primary” residence in mortgage applications in 2021. Mortgages on primary homes can often receive a lower interest rate or other beneficial terms.

“An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing,” Lowell and Eisen said in August.
The Federal Reserve declined to comment on Trump’s announcement.

Trump launches new effort to oust Fed Governor Lisa Cook
By Elisabeth Buchwald, Matt Egan, CNN
(CNN) — President Donald Trump is mounting a fresh offensive in his battle to oust Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, forming a committee of his own appointees to investigate allegations against her.
The committee will investigate alleged false statements Cook made in connection with mortgages on two properties and hold an in-person hearing at the White House on November 5, the White House announced on Friday.
Analysts say the formation of the committee and setting of a hearing date indicate Trump officials are addressing procedural issues addressed by a June Supreme Court ruling that initially blocked the administration from removing Cook.
Newly installed Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, who is also serving as acting director of the Office of Government Ethics, is one of the three members. So is National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett, a staunch defender of Trump’s economic agenda, whom the president considered for Fed chair. The third member is Andrea Lucas, chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.
Cook’s attorneys, Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen, said they have been in touch with the White House “to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box-checking exercise.”
“Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her,” they said in a statement provided to CNN on Friday.
The formation of the committee marks the latest salvo in Trump’s ongoing attempts to reshape the Fed and comes just weeks ahead of its next monetary policy meeting, where officials will consider whether interest rate changes are merited.
“This seems tailor-made to address the Supreme Court’s biggest criticism in its last attempt: that Governor Cook didn’t have a chance to defend herself,” said Tim Mahedy, a former official at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, who is now CEO of research firm Access/Macro.
Mahedy said the outcome of this review “is clear” given the makeup of the committee. He expressed surprise that Hassett, a White House economist, would be on a committee investigating a legal matter about paperwork.
Trump has long berated the politically independent Fed because it hasn’t lowered interest rates to his liking, publicly targeting Cook and former Fed Chair Jerome Powell. But Trump has spared the current chairman, Kevin Warsh, whom he appointed to the position earlier this year after Powell’s term at the head of the central bank expired. Instead, Trump has insisted that Warsh is blocked by a “political” Board of Governors.
The central bank’s eight-member Board votes on interest rate decisions, along with regional Fed presidents. While the Fed leader often plays an influential role in shaping the discussion on policy moves, decisions are ultimately the result of the 12-person committee process.
At its September meeting, all 12 members, including Warsh, voted to raise rates for the first time in three years in an effort to contain inflation that has heated up largely due to the US war with Iran.
Trump said later that Warsh shouldn’t have greenlit a rate hike. “I don’t blame Kevin Warsh. I probably would have voted against the Board if I were him,” Trump said in an interview Time Magazine published earlier this month.
Separately, Trump reaffirmed he wants Warsh to “vote the way he wants.”
Trump vs. Cook
Trump previously sought to fire Cook over unproven allegations of mortgage fraud. Ultimately, in a 5-4 decision earlier this year, the Supreme Court ruled Trump could not immediately remove her.
“The 5-4 Supreme Court decision did not prohibit President Trump from firing a Fed Governor, it gave him a roadmap to do it,” Ed Mills, Washington policy analyst at Raymond James, told CNN in an email.
Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in his majority opinion released in June that Cook was entitled to sufficient time and notice to respond to a termination and that she wasn’t given a fair opportunity to respond last year when Trump initially sought to remove her.
But that doesn’t mean Trump can’t lawfully fire her, he said. The law allows a president to remove Fed governors “for cause,” which is generally interpreted to mean negligence or malfeasance in the role.
The “ultimate question of whether the president can remove Cook for cause will depend in part on the underlying facts,” Roberts wrote. “We have not addressed the facts, as they have yet to be found or analyzed under the relevant legal standards.”
Mills said Cook is “very clearly at risk of being fired, and it is unclear if the Supreme Court would block President Trump in Round 2.”
He added that two of Cook’s colleagues, Powell and Governor Michael Barr, are also on the list for “potential ‘for-cause’ firing.”
Kurt Lewis, a former special adviser to Powell who is now head of central bank policy at Piper Sandler, said this will ultimately come down to how much deference the Supreme Court gives the president on “cause” once justices think he has “followed a semblance of procedure.”
Cook was appointed by former President Joe Biden in 2022 and is the first Black female Fed governor, with a term set to expire in 2038.

Cook has consistently maintained that she did nothing wrong.
Just weeks ago, Cook’s lawyer told the White House for a second time that, “There is no legal basis for President Trump to remove Governor Cook for cause.”
“An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing,” Abbe Lowell said Aug. 26. “These attacks on Governor Cook are not about real estate paperwork; they are an attempt by President Trump to force the Federal Reserve to bend to his will.”

Authored by Zachary Stieber via The Epoch Times,
President Donald Trump on Oct. 9 announced a new committee to investigate whether a Federal Reserve governor made false statements.
The committee will probe allegations that Lisa Cook, governor of the Federal Reserve, offered false information in connection with at least one mortgage instrument, Trump said in a presidential memorandum establishing the panel.
The Federal Reserve is the country's central banking system. Cook, 62, was appointed as its governor in 2022 and confirmed by the Senate.
Depending on the findings, there may be cause to remove Cook, Trump said.
Kevin Hassett, an adviser to Trump; Keith Sonderling, acting director of the U.S. Office of Government Ethics; and Andrea Lucas, chair of the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, are members of the committee.
An in-person hearing to consider evidence in the case will take place on Nov. 5 at the White House, according to the memorandum. Cook was invited to submit a written statement regarding the allegations and can appear at the hearing if she wishes.
The committee can question Cook about any representations she or her lawyers make during the hearing and request documents from her. Cook shall comply with such requests, Trump said.
A lawyer representing Cook did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Trump tried firing Cook in 2025, alleging that she had committed "deceitful and potentially criminal conduct in a financial matter."
He pointed to a criminal referral made by William Pulte, director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency. The referral said Cook wrote in one document that a property in Michigan would be her primary residence for the following year but two weeks later signed a separate document attesting that a property in Georgia would be her primary residence for the next 12 months.
Chief Justice John Roberts, writing the majority, turned down arguments from the government, including that the removal was not judicially removal and that even if it was, the requirements for such a removal were met.
Ruling for the government would change the "for cause" protection outlined in federal law for the position into "at-will employment," which was "out of step with the statute Congress enacted and our Nation's tradition of central banking protected from political interference," Roberts wrote at the time.
Lawyers for Cook responded by saying the allegations were baseless and amounted to interfering with the Federal Reserve's independence.
"No matter what President Trump tries to do next, this much is clear under the facts and Supreme Court precedent - there is no valid cause for removing Governor Cook. As we did before, we will challenge this latest pretext and preserve her position and the historic role of the Fed," they said.

Trump Creates Lisa Cook Inquiry Committee in Renewed Bid to Remove Fed Governor/ TezzBuzz/ WASHINGTON/ J. Mansour/ President Donald Trump established a committee Friday to investigate allegations that Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook made false statements on mortgage applications. His memorandum calls for Cook to attend a private White House hearing Nov. 5, with a transcript published afterward. Cook denies wrongdoing, and her attorneys are evaluating the process following a Supreme Court ruling that allowed her to remain in office.
Quick Look
- New inquiry: Trump created a committee to examine mortgage application allegations against Cook.
- Hearing date: His memo directs her to appear at the White House Nov. 5.
- Public access: The hearing would be closed, but a transcript would be released.
- Defense response: Cook’s lawyers say she welcomes a chance to present facts but question whether the process will be genuine.

Deep Look
Trump Establishes Committee to Investigate Lisa Cook
President Donald Trump renewed his effort to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook Friday, establishing a “committee of inquiry” to investigate allegations involving her mortgage applications.
A presidential memorandum calls for a Nov. 5 hearing at the White House and says Cook “shall” attend to answer the committee’s questions.
The hearing would not be public, although a transcript would be published afterward.
The initiative marks another stage in the first presidential attempt to remove a Fed governor in the central bank’s 113-year history.
White House Demand Raises Fed Independence Concerns
The demand that Cook testify before a presidential committee is likely to renew concerns about the Federal Reserve’s independence.
Trump has urged the central bank to lower its benchmark interest rate. Instead, the Fed raised it last month under Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom Trump appointed earlier this year.
“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump wrote in the memorandum.
Cook’s Attorneys Evaluate Proposed Hearing
Cook’s lawyers, Abbe Lowell and Norman Eisen, said they were considering whether she would attend the hearing and respond to the allegations.
“We have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise,” they said in a statement. “Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her.”
Cook denies wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.
Mortgage Applications Underlie Removal Effort
Trump first attempted to fire Cook in August 2025, alleging she committed mortgage fraud by identifying two properties as her “primary” residence in 2021 loan applications.
Loans for primary residences can carry lower interest rates or other favorable terms.
Lowell and Eisen have previously described the discrepancy as an “inadvertent error” and said Cook identified one property as a vacation home in other documents.
“An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing,” the attorneys said in August.
Cook Participated in Unanimous September Rate Increase
Trump and some economic advisers have blamed the Fed’s broader rate-setting committee for the recent increase in borrowing costs.
That committee includes 19 officials, with 12 voting members. Cook holds a voting seat as a member of the Fed’s seven-member Board of Governors.
The Sept. 16 decision to raise rates was unanimous.

The president created a new committee to investigate Fed Gov. Lisa Cook. Plus, NAR backs independent contractor bill; HUD launches fair housing inquiry; more.
This week in Washington, D.C., the conflict between President Donald Trump and Federal Reserve Gov. Lisa Cook escalated again with the announcement that Trump has created a committee to investigate the central bank official.
Elsewhere in the nation's capital, Freddie Mac has experienced another leadership shakeup, and the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) said it plans to cut the budget for its independent watchdog arm.
Meanwhile, HUD is launching a new investigation into Wells Fargo over alleged Fair Housing Act violations. And in a potentially positive development for real estate professionals, two U.S. senators have introduced legislation that would recognize agents as independent contractors under federal law.
White House committee to investigate mortgage fraud allegations
On Oct. 7, Trump issued a memorandum announcing the establishment of a committee of inquiry to investigate allegations that Cook "made false statements in connection with one or more mortgage instruments." Trump and others within his administration have accused Cook of lying on mortgage applications prior to her time at the Fed. Trump attempted to fire her last year over her alleged actions.
Cook, who has not been charged with a crime, has denied any wrongdoing and sued to keep her job. The Supreme Court in June allowed Cook to continue serving on the central bank's board of governors while her lawsuit against the president proceeds.
In the memorandum, Trump instructed the new committee to "investigate the allegations against Governor Cook and report to me whether there is 'cause' for Governor Cook's removal." It also scheduled an in-person hearing to "consider the evidence and allegations" on Nov. 5.
In a statement to The New York Times, attorneys representing Cook expressed "grave doubts that this 'hearing' is a legitimate one that would conform to the law." If, however, the committee's investigation is objective, "the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board," they added.
NAR backs bill that would codify agents as independent contractors
This week, NAR applauded the introduction of new legislation that would affirm agents' roles as independent contractors.
On Sept. 30, Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah introduced the Direct Seller and Real Estate Agent Harmonization Act, which is co-sponsored by fellow Utah Sen. John Curtis. A companion bill was introduced in the House last year by Rep. Kevin Kiley, a California independent.
The Senate bill would ensure that federal law recognizes agents as independent contractors, a change that Lee said would give them "clear legal status."
In an Oct. 6 statement, NAR EVP and Chief Advocacy Officer Shannon McGahn added that the legislation would "provide important clarity under the Fair Labor Standards Act and ensure real estate professionals are treated fairly and consistently under federal law."
"Independent contractors are a vital part of the real estate economy," McGahn said, "and this legislation affirms their role while reducing unnecessary confusion and regulatory burdens."
HUD launches probe over alleged Fair Housing Act violations
HUD is investigating whether Wells Fargo's attempts to boost homeownership among Black Americans violated the Fair Housing Act. The Wall Street Journal was first to cover the investigation's launch.
In an Oct. 7 letter to Wells Fargo's chairman and CEO, HUD Assistant Secretary for Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity Craig Trainor cited alleged actions by the bank to offer products or product terms "based on race" during former President Joe Biden's administration.
"In response to your bank's repeated public promotion of explicit race-based lending policies, I have directed the Office of Special Investigations to investigate Wells Fargo for potential fair housing violations," Trainor wrote, adding that his office "may file a complaint" against the company depending on the outcome of its investigation.
HUD Secretary Scott Turner suggested in an Oct. 7 statement that, regardless of whether Wells Fargo violated the law, "its practice of dividing Americans based on race is immoral, unethical and un-American."

Anil Hinduja, an executive who has been with Freddie Mac for over a decade, no longer works for the enterprise, according to a Sept. 30 filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Why it matters for us
The Fed sets interest rates, which touch mortgages, car loans, credit cards, and small business lending. If a president can remove governors at will, the central bank stops being independent and starts being political, and rate decisions start answering to whoever is in the White House instead of the economy. A successful removal would shrink that already small circle of representation at the top of American economic policy, and it would send a signal about how much independence any institution keeps when it conflicts with the president.
