sources.news_title: Trump Committee to Investigate, Remove Fed's Lisa Cook
sources.text:
President Donald Trump signed a presidential memorandum on October 7, 2026, creating a “Trump Committee to Investigate” whether Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook “made false statements in connection with one or more mortgage instruments.” The committee, announced publicly by the White House on October 9, will gather evidence, hold a hearing on November 5, 2026, and recommend whether there is legal “cause” to remove Cook from the Fed’s Board of Governors. The move follows a failed 2025 firing attempt and a landmark Supreme Court ruling that said Cook cannot be removed without due process.
Who Is Lisa Cook and What Does She Do at the Fed?
Lisa Cook is one of seven governors on the Federal Reserve’s Board of Governors, the body that sets U.S. monetary policy, including interest rates that affect everything from Utica mortgage payments to small-business loans. She was originally nominated by President Joe Biden, confirmed to a full 14-year term in 2023, and is one of the few Black women ever to serve on the board.
Cook is an economist with a background in macroeconomics and economic history. Before joining the Fed, she was a professor at Michigan State University and held roles at the Treasury Department and the Council of Economic Advisers. Her term as a governor would ordinarily run well into the 2030s, which is precisely why Trump’s effort to remove her is so significant: governors are meant to be insulated from political pressure by design.
Why Does Trump Want to Remove Lisa Cook From the Federal Reserve?
Trump’s stated reason is mortgage fraud. The allegations center on loan applications for two homes, one in Georgia and one in Michigan, where Trump’s allies accuse Cook of declaring both properties as her “primary residence” to secure better mortgage terms, as The Hill reported. A referral from Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte reportedly pushed the White House toward the investigation.
The deeper context matters. Trump has spent his second term waging a public pressure campaign against the Fed, repeatedly demanding lower interest rates. Cook, like other governors, has defended the central bank’s independence. Critics see the mortgage allegations as a pretext, a way to convert a political disagreement into a removable “for cause” offense. As of early October 2026, Cook has not been charged with any crime, and multiple outlets stress the fraud claims remain unproven, per AP’s reporting.
What Powers Does the President Have to Remove Fed Board Members?
Legally, a president cannot simply fire a Fed governor at will. The Federal Reserve Act allows removal only “for cause”, traditionally understood as negligence, misconduct, or dereliction of duty, not policy disagreements. That protection exists so monetary policy isn’t subject to presidential mood swings.
The Supreme Court reinforced that framework in Trump v. Cook, 146 S. Ct. 2234 (2026). In a 5-4 decision issued in June 2026, the Court held that Cook was entitled to notice and an opportunity to respond before any removal. A footnote in the ruling noted that Trump could “try again” if he followed due-process requirements, effectively inviting the committee process now underway, as CNN explained.
Can the Fed Chair or President Fire a Federal Reserve Governor?
No single official can unilaterally fire a Fed governor. The president nominates governors, the Senate confirms them, and removal requires legally sufficient “cause.” Fed Chair Jerome Powell, for his part, cannot remove a fellow governor either. The only path runs through the president, and only after a fact-finding and legal process that courts will scrutinize.
What Is the Process for Removing Someone From the Federal Reserve Board?
The memorandum lays out a specific sequence, according to the official White House presidential action:
- Committee formation. The attorney general and other senior administration officials assemble the panel of inquiry.
- Written response. Cook must submit a written statement answering the allegations.
- Hearing. Cook must appear in person at the White House on November 5, 2026, where committee members “consider the evidence and allegations against Governor Cook.”
- Findings. The committee must produce written findings of fact, conclusions of law, and a recommendation on whether cause exists to remove her.
- Presidential decision. Trump then decides whether to act on the recommendation, and any removal would almost certainly be challenged in court.
Common mistake to avoid: don’t confuse this committee with a criminal prosecution. It is an internal executive-branch process, not a court. Cook faces no criminal charges, and the committee’s findings are political-legal recommendations, not verdicts.
Has a Fed Board Member Ever Been Removed Before?
No. This is the first time in the Federal Reserve’s 113-year history that a president has attempted to fire a sitting governor, making the episode unprecedented by definition. Governors have resigned, retired, and been renominated or passed over, but none has been forcibly removed.
That historical blank slate is exactly why legal analysts describe the stakes as enormous. There is no precedent guiding how courts should weigh a president’s removal power against the Fed’s statutory independence, which is why the Supreme Court’s 2026 ruling and whatever comes next will shape the boundaries of presidential authority for decades.
What Are Lisa Cook’s Qualifications and Background?
Cook’s resume is, by any conventional standard, strong. She holds a doctorate in economics from the University of California, Berkeley. She taught at Michigan State University, served on the faculty of Harvard’s Kennedy School, and worked at the Treasury Department and the Council of Economic Advisers under both parties. Her research has examined economic growth, financial crises, and the economic costs of racial violence.
That background is worth remembering when assessing the “for cause” question. The allegations against her do not concern her conduct as a Fed governor, her votes, her analysis, or her stewardship of monetary policy. They concern personal mortgage applications filed before her service on the board, which is one reason critics call the process politically motivated.
How Long Is a Fed Governor’s Term, and When Does Cook’s End?
Fed governors serve staggered 14-year terms, a design meant to outlast any single president. Cook’s full term would run into the 2030s. Trump’s effort to shorten it is the point of conflict: he would need to establish legal cause, not simply wait out the calendar or express disagreement with her policy positions.
What Would Happen if Lisa Cook Is Removed From the Fed?
If the committee finds cause and Trump removes her, expect immediate litigation. Related proceedings are already pending in U.S. District Court, and analysts anticipate the issue would return to the Supreme Court, as CNBC reported. The committee’s findings would become the central evidence in that fight.
The practical consequences reach beyond one governor. Markets watch Fed independence closely. If investors believe governors can be fired for politically unpopular votes, they may price in faster, politically timed rate cuts, which typically means higher inflation risk and higher long-term borrowing costs for families and businesses, including here in the Mohawk Valley.
Is It Legal for Trump to Set Up a Committee to Investigate Fed Officials?
That’s the contested question. Trump’s memorandum cites his authority under the Federal Reserve Act and the Supreme Court’s own framework, which requires notice and an opportunity to respond before removal. On paper, the committee is that process.
But critics point to a structural problem: the committee is composed of Trump appointees and senior officials loyal to the administration, with the president controlling both the fact-finding and the legal conclusions, as The Washington Post noted. A process where the prosecutor, judge, and jury all answer to the accuser is one courts may view skeptically. Expect Cook’s lawyers to make exactly that argument if removal follows.
What Other Fed Members Might Trump Target for Removal?
Cook isn’t the only name in play. Trump has also tangled with Governor Michael Barr, and allies previously floated a criminal case against former Chair Jerome Powell tied to costly renovations at Fed facilities. That avenue has now closed: an inspector general review of the renovations concluded without findings supporting criminal charges, and the Justice Department declined to reopen the matter, per Politico.
The pattern is consistent: pressure the Fed toward lower rates, and use whatever tool is available against officials who resist. Trump’s history of testing institutional limits is well documented, see our earlier coverage of how Trump drew attention with an admission he fired Comey and his baseless claims about the California recall election.
How Has the Fed Responded to Trump’s Investigation Committee?
The Fed board itself has largely declined to comment on personnel matters, while Cook has continued to serve and participate in policy votes. Her legal team fought the August 2025 firing attempt all the way to the Supreme Court and won on due-process grounds. The White House statement frames the committee as routine fact-finding; Cook’s allies frame it as a second, more carefully dressed attempt at the same outcome.
FAQ
Can Trump fire Lisa Cook outright?
Not without a legal process. The Supreme Court ruled in June 2026 that Cook is entitled to notice and an opportunity to respond before removal. The committee is Trump’s attempt to satisfy that requirement.
What is Lisa Cook accused of?
Trump’s allies allege she declared two homes, in Georgia and Michigan, as her “primary residence” on mortgage applications to obtain better terms. She has not been charged with any crime, and the allegations remain unproven.
When is Cook’s hearing?
The memorandum requires her to appear before the committee at the White House on November 5, 2026, after submitting a written statement.
Has a president ever tried to remove a Fed governor before?
No. This is the first such attempt in the Federal Reserve’s 113-year history.
What does “for cause” removal mean?
It means removal for misconduct, negligence, or dereliction of duty, not for policy disagreements. That standard is central to whether the committee’s findings could survive a court challenge.
Could Cook’s removal affect interest rates?
Indirectly, yes. If governors fear removal for politically unpopular votes, the Fed’s independence erodes, and markets may expect politically timed rate cuts, with inflation risks that follow.
What happens after the committee reports?
Trump decides whether to remove Cook. Any removal would trigger litigation in federal court, likely returning eventually to the Supreme Court.
Conclusion
The committee announced on October 9, 2026 is not the end of this fight, it’s the opening of a new chapter in an unprecedented constitutional standoff. A president is attempting, for the first time in the Fed’s 113-year history, to remove a sitting governor, using a panel of his own appointees to generate the legal justification. Whatever the committee concludes on November 5, the real verdict will come from the courts, and possibly from voters who understand that central bank independence protects their savings, their mortgages, and their paychecks.
Here’s what readers can do: follow the November 5 hearing and the committee’s findings as they emerge; contact Senators Schumer and Gillibrand to ask how they plan to respond to what happens next; and share accurate reporting, like AP’s coverage and NBC News’s reporting, with neighbors who may only be seeing headlines. Institutions don’t defend themselves. An informed public does.

Lowell and Eisen added: “We have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box-checking exercise. Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her.”
False Statements Alleged
Trump first tried to fire Cook last year, after administration officials raised allegations that she made false statements on at least one mortgage-related document, CNBC reported.
Cook has denied wrongdoing and filed a lawsuit to block her dismissal. A federal court temporarily barred Trump from firing her, and the Supreme Court narrowly upheld that ruling in June.
The Supreme Court did not stop Trump from trying again for Cook’s removal.
The high court rejected the president’s first bid because Cook was not given proper legal due process, and said any new attempt to fire her would require additional steps.
Under the Federal Reserve Act, a president can remove a Fed governor only “for cause,” CNBC reported.
In August, White House aide Dan Scavino told Cook in a letter that the president was again “considering” firing her in connection with the mortgage allegations.
“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump states in the memo establishing the committee of inquiry. The memo is addressed to Attorney General Todd Blanche.
Senator Assails Trump
“To assist me in carrying out that responsibility, the Committee shall investigate the allegations against Governor Cook and report to me whether there is ‘cause’ for Governor Cook’s removal,” within the meaning identified by the Supreme Court, it says.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., in a statement accused Trump of “convening an illegitimate show trial in his dangerous quest to illegally take over our nation’s central bank.”
“Instead of playing judge in a kangaroo court of his own making, Trump should end the war in Iran and cancel his chaotic tariffs,” said Warren, the top-ranking Democrat on the Senate’s Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.

sources.text:
Donald Trump announced on Friday that he is establishing a committee to investigate Lisa Cook, the US Federal Reserve governor, over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, renewing his efforts to oust her despite a June supreme court ruling that her earlier firing was unconstitutional.
Trump said a committee will consult with justice department officials to decide whether there is “cause” for her removal. The White House will hold an in-person hearing on 5 November to consider the allegations against Cook, which will be closed to the public but transcribed and published. Cook will be able to submit a written statement to present her own evidence and will be subject to examination from White House and her own legal counsel.
“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump said in a statement posted to the White House’s website.
Cook’s battle with the White House began in August 2025 when she was abruptly fired after Trump said she committed mortgage fraud by listing two properties in Georgia and Michigan as her primary residence and failing to report rental income on her Atlanta property.
Her legal team has maintained that the White House is “cherrypicking” facts and any claims of fraud are based on unrelated clerical errors.
Cook immediately sued the Trump administration, and the supreme court reinstated her after a 5-4 ruling that she could stay on as governor while fighting the fraud allegations.
In June, the court ruled that Trump’s firing was unconstitutional because he did not follow proper procedure and give Cook an opportunity to dispute the allegations before she was fired.
Cook was fired just as Trump was launching unprecedented attacks on the Fed’s chair, then Jerome Powell, in his blustering push to get the central bank to lower interest rates. Trump also launched a justice department investigation into Powell, which was dropped in April.
Congress created the Fed to be an independent and nonpartisan institution. Economists widely agree that a central bank unswayed by politics is essential for the stability of a country’s economy.
Kevin Warsh, Powell’s successor, has repeatedly faced questions over how he will maintain the Fed’s independence. Before Trump picked him to lead the world’s most powerful central bank, he had echoed the president’s calls for cutting rates. But because of elevated inflation brought on by the war in the Middle East, the bank ultimately voted to raise rates in its last meeting, which drew the ire of the White House just more than a month before the crucial midterm elections.
